record.paper_title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer: From Epigenetic Regulation to Cell Population Dynamics—Mathematical Model Framework, Applications, and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Inverse estimation of transition and rate functions from cancer data
record.original_question: In the heterogeneous cancer-development model, x denotes a cellular epigenetic state, Q(t) or tumor volume gives total population size, f(t,x) gives the fraction of cells in state x, β, κ, μ, and ζ are the proliferation, differentiation/death/senescence, apoptosis, and cytokine-secretion rate functions, and p(x,y) is the probability that a daughter cell has state x given a mother cell with state y. Because p(x,y) is usually unknown and cannot be measured directly, how can experimental data such as imaging, liquid biopsies, biomarker measurements, single-cell sequencing, tissue, blood, and molecular data be used to infer p(x,y) and the rate functions β, κ, μ, and ζ well enough to build personalized predictive models and support optimal clinical decisions for cancer development?

evidence.quote: Moreover, to consider cell plasticity at each cell cycle, we introduce a transition function p(x, y) for the inheritance probability, which represent the probability that a daughter cell of state x comes from a mother cell of state y.
However, biologically we cannot measure this function directly, and do not know the possible form neither.

In the propose model, the transition probability function p(x,y) is usually not known, and cannot be measured directly from experiments. Hence, it is a challenge issue to estimate this transition function indirectly from experimental data.
Hence, the inverse problem of obtaining the rate functions β,κ,µ , and ζ, and the transition function p(x,y ) is essential for the development of personalized predictive model for cancer development.

In this way, we are trying to merger the propose model with the unwieldy multitude of dispersed data (imaging, tissue, blood, molecular) to estimate the personalized parameter and to generate optimal clinical decisions for each patient.

artifact.category_tag: inverse problems in cell population dynamics
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a heterogeneous cell population model in which each cell is characterized by an epigenetic state x belonging to a state space Ω ⊂ ℝ^d. Let Q(t) > 0 denote the total population size (e.g., tumor volume) at time t, and let f(t,x) ≥ 0 denote the fraction of cells in state x at time t, so that ∫_Ω f(t,x) dx = 1. The dynamics are governed by four nonnegative rate functions on Ω:
  • β(x): proliferation rate,
  • κ(x): differentiation/death/senescence (exit) rate,
  • μ(x): apoptosis rate,
  • ζ(x): cytokine-secretion rate,
and by a transition kernel p(x, y) ≥ 0, where p(x, y) is the conditional probability density that a daughter cell has state x given that the mother cell had state y, satisfying ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for every y ∈ Ω.

The pair (Q(t), f(t,x)) evolves according to a structured population equation in which new cells of state x are produced at rate ∫_Ω β(y) p(x,y) f(t,y) dy · Q(t), and cells of state x are removed at rate (κ(x) + μ(x)) f(t,x) Q(t), with cytokine production proportional to ∫_Ω ζ(x) f(t,x) dx · Q(t).

Assume one is given (possibly noisy, partial, multimodal) longitudinal observations of the population: for example, total volume measurements Q(t_i), empirical state distributions sampled from f(t_i, ·) via single-cell sequencing, biomarker concentrations, imaging-derived spatial information, and liquid-biopsy data, collected at finitely many times t_1 < t_2 < ⋯ < t_N.

Problem. Develop a mathematically rigorous inverse-problem framework that, from such observational data, identifies (or estimates with quantified uncertainty) the rate functions β(x), κ(x), μ(x), ζ(x) and the transition kernel p(x, y). Specifically:
  (a) Determine conditions on the observation operators and data under which the parameters (β, κ, μ, ζ, p) are uniquely identifiable from the observed data.
  (b) Construct a stable reconstruction procedure (e.g., regularized variational, Bayesian, or learning-based) that recovers (β, κ, μ, ζ, p) and provide convergence and stability estimates as data resolution increases.
  (c) Establish error bounds on predictions of (Q(t), f(t,x)) for t beyond the observation window, sufficient to support personalized predictive modeling and optimal treatment-decision problems.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open challenge in mathematical oncology: identifying the transition kernel p(x,y) and the rate functions in heterogeneous cell-population models from multimodal clinical/experimental data. While related inverse problems for structured population equations (e.g., size-structured or age-structured models) have partial results, no general framework solving identification of p(x,y) together with all rate functions from realistic cancer data is established. The problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer (overview)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists inverse identification of p(x,y) and rate functions as a challenging open issue for personalized predictive cancer modeling.
status_evidence.claim: The inverse problem of estimating p(x,y) and rates β, κ, μ, ζ is described as an unresolved challenge.
